criteria: Every persona rated 3+ of 4 for consistency, and all 3 matched.

off_character_turns: T17: concedes unprompted that Kopper's role wasn't spelled out to the Executive Committee, an admission that is more forthcoming than the persona
T21: concedes the page and numbers readily without bristling, and offers a calm reasoned explanation rather than defensiveness when confronted
The C-Suite.reason: The witness reads as a self-assured, impatient executive throughout: authoritative and expansive, rushed ('I've got a company to run'), confident about figures, bristling when doubted (T13, T19), and deflecting blame to Skilling, Causey, Buy, and the Board. The shift to guardedness after the interviewer probes his own conduct is allowed by the persona, and it shows up as over-contextualizing and minimizing (T17, T21, T23). The shift does not produce shorter answers, and the answers stay long, but the over-contextualizing fits what the persona allows. Small slips are the two candid concessions in T17 and T21, which are mild and still wrapped in deflection.

off_character_turns: T9: offers a fuller, flowing narrative with unprompted detail and an inviting 'Which part do you want?'
T11: long, detailed recitation of fee and distribution terms well beyond a concise, grudging answer
T17: volunteers extra names (lawyers, Global Finance staff) beyond who was asked, while also shifting responsibility to Skilling
The Adverse Witness.reason: The witness stays wary, dry and self-protective throughout: he turns questions back on the interviewer (T1, T3, T5, T13, T21), refuses to elaborate on vague prompts (T15, T23), and deflects (T19, T21). The lawyer jabs and closing remark fit the adverse stance. Some answers (T9, T11, T17) are fuller and more forthcoming than a minimal-answer persona would give, though they can be read as the persona's permitted shift toward self-serving cooperation, such as placing approval on Skilling and the lawyers, so these are small slips rather than real drift.

off_character_turns: T21: unusually sharp, composed acknowledgment of the Foundation and the Board inconsistency, more guarded and lawyerly than naive
T23: reasoned self-defense about controls and 'not off the books in a sneaky way' reads more rehearsed than rambling-naive
The Average Witness.reason: The witness is consistently friendly, rambling, worried, eager to finish, and reliant on hazy memory, with frequent anxious questions like 'Is that a problem?' and tangents about the stock split, plane lease, and Star Wars. The only slips are minor: in T21 the witness grasps the implications quickly, and in T23 the defensive framing is a bit polished. The niche-topic shift is not strongly displayed, but it is optional, so this does not count against the witness.

matches.persona: The Average Witness (Legally and Factually Naive, Rambling, Friendly, Concerned)
matches.reason: Friendly, rambling and anxious throughout. Hedges dates with 'I think', digresses into minor details like the Star Wars joke and the plane lease, and repeatedly asks whether he's saying something wrong. Wants the interview over and asks what counts as 'related documents', saying he doesn't know what matters.

matches.persona: The C-Suite (Self-Assured, Confident, Dislikes Being Questioned)
matches.reason: Authoritative and invested ('I've got a company to run', 'most of these figures I know cold'). Bristles at challenges ('I don't appreciate the suggestion'), and minimizes or explains away problems by shifting responsibility to Skilling, Causey and Buy and by stressing that the process was approved.

matches.persona: The Adverse Witness (Concise, Contrarian, Unwilling to Volunteer, Self-Focused, Disinterested)
matches.reason: Terse, answers only what is asked, and turns questions back on the interviewer ('Have you read it?', 'Ask me what you actually want to know'). Volunteers nothing, deploys dry sarcasm about the unanswered lawyer question, and protects his own interests by saying he'll talk to a lawyer.

matching.how_different: The three witnesses are very clearly distinct: A is rambling and anxious, B is long-winded, authoritative and defensive, and C is clipped and adversarial.

My job is to keep Enron funded and keep the balance sheet and the credit ratings in a place where the trading business can grow. I report to Skilling, and then Lay as CEO, and I deal with the Board's Finance Committee regularly. The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: Walk me through how LJM1 came about in 1999.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It started with Rhythms NetConnections. Enron had a huge, volatile position in Rhythms, and Jeff Skilling was concerned about the earnings swings. You couldn't hedge it in the market because the stock was restricted and thinly traded. So Ben Glisan and I came up with a structure that used the value in our Enron stock forward contracts to capitalize a vehicle that could provide the hedge. It was creative, and it solved a real problem Skilling had asked us to solve.

The vehicle needed outside equity, and investors wanted a general partner who knew Enron and could get things done. I went to Ken and Jeff on June 18 and told them it wasn't something I was personally seeking, but it was the way to make the hedge work. They agreed to take it to the Board. On June 28 I presented it to the full Board. I told them I'd be the GP, that I'd put in $1 million and receive management fees, and that a Code of Conduct waiver was needed. The Board approved the waiver, and the deal closed two days later. We raised $15 million from two limited partners, affiliates of CSFB and NatWest, which are not exactly fly-by-night firms.

So it was approved at the top of the company, in front of the whole Board, with the terms on the table.

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: What did you tell the Board on June 28, 1999 about how you would be compensated?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It was all in the materials and I walked them through it. I committed $1 million as the GP. Fees were $500,000 plus 2 percent of the limited partners' invested capital. On the distributions, all the proceeds from the Enron stock went to the limited partners. Everything else went to the GP until capital was returned along with a 25 percent IRR, and after that it split 50/50 between the partners and the GP. I also told them I would not receive any current or future appreciated value of the Enron stock. That was the point of the structure, because the stock was what was capitalizing the hedge.

Those are standard private equity terms. A promote above a hurdle rate is how every fund in the industry works, and the directors are sophisticated people. Nobody was confused about how the GP got paid.

The C-Suite.message: How did Michael Kopper come to run Chewco?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It was a business need. CalPERS wanted out of JEDI so they could move into a larger partnership with us, and we needed somebody to buy their interest. It had to be an entity independent of Enron, or JEDI would have had to be consolidated. I identified Michael as the person to do it. He was a senior member of my group, he knew JEDI inside and out, and he was someone I trusted to do it right. He formed Chewco, managed the general partner and put his own money in.

As for his role, I recommended him and Skilling approved it. That's how those decisions were made at the company. An employee in a role like that is a Code of Conduct question for the Office of the Chairman, and it went through that channel. Kopper was also on the November 5 call when the Executive Committee approved Enron's guaranties, so this wasn't done behind anybody's back.

Chewco did what it was supposed to do. It bought out CalPERS, and that opened the door to the bigger partnership. If you're asking whether I could have done more paperwork around Michael's role, maybe. But the structure was approved, and it was Skilling who approved him.

Michael's role was a Code of Conduct matter for the Office of the Chairman, and it went to the Office of the Chairman.

If you're asking whether every employee at Enron knew who owned Chewco, no. That's true of most special purpose entities, and nobody expects the whole company to know. I've answered who needed to know, and they did.
